first_memory.longDescription: CLAUDE.md files are Claude Code's persistent memory system. When you create your first CLAUDE.md, you're establishing a foundation for Claude to understand your preferences, project context, and working style across all future sessions. This file persists between conversations, unlike chat history which resets.
first_memory.whyItMatters: Without persistent memory, Claude starts fresh every session. CLAUDE.md ensures your preferences and project knowledge carry forward automatically.

howTo.summary: Create a CLAUDE.md file at your project root or in ~/.claude/ for global settings.

steps.instruction: Create a project-level CLAUDE.md in your repository root

code.content: touch CLAUDE.md

steps.instruction: Add some basic project context that Claude should remember

code.content:
# Project Context

This is a Node.js API using Express and PostgreSQL.

## Important Files
- src/index.ts - Main entry point
- src/routes/ - API routes

examples.title: Minimal CLAUDE.md

code.content:
# My Project

This is a React TypeScript project using Vite.

## Conventions
- Use functional components
- Prefer CSS modules over styled-components

examples.explanation: Even a few lines helps Claude understand your project better.

tips: Start simple and add more as you discover what Claude needs to remember

project_memory.longDescription: A project CLAUDE.md lives in your repository root and contains project-specific instructions that apply only to that codebase. This separates project conventions from your personal preferences, making it easy to share with teammates or switch between different projects with different coding standards.
project_memory.whyItMatters: Project-level memory keeps your team aligned. Everyone using Claude Code on the same repo gets the same context and conventions automatically.

howTo.summary: Create a CLAUDE.md file in the root of your project directory.

steps.instruction: Navigate to your project root and create the file

code.content:
cd /path/to/your/project
touch CLAUDE.md

steps.instruction: Add project-specific information Claude should know

code.content:
# Project Guidelines

## Tech Stack
- Frontend: React 18 with TypeScript
- Backend: Node.js with Express
- Database: PostgreSQL with Prisma ORM

## Code Style
- Use 2-space indentation
- Prefer async/await over .then()
- All components must have unit tests

examples.title: Full-stack project memory

code.content:
# E-commerce Platform

## Architecture
- Monorepo using Turborepo
- packages/web - Next.js frontend
- packages/api - Express backend
- packages/shared - Shared types and utilities

## Development
- Run `pnpm dev` to start all services

examples.explanation: Comprehensive project context helps Claude navigate large codebases effectively.

tips: Commit CLAUDE.md to version control so your team shares the same context
Keep it focused on what Claude needs, not general documentation

personal_scribe.longDescription: Your user-level CLAUDE.md at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md contains personal preferences that apply across all projects. This is where you define your universal coding style, communication preferences, and any global behaviors you want Claude to follow regardless of which project you're working on.
personal_scribe.whyItMatters: Personal memory means you don't repeat yourself. Set your preferences once, and they apply everywhere automatically.

howTo.summary: Create a CLAUDE.md file in your ~/.claude/ directory for global preferences.

steps.instruction: Create the .claude directory and personal memory file

code.content:
mkdir -p ~/.claude
touch ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md

steps.instruction: Add your personal coding preferences and style

code.content:
# Personal Preferences

## Communication Style
- Be concise, skip unnecessary explanations
- Don't use emojis unless I ask

## Code Style
- I prefer TypeScript over JavaScript
- Always use const over let when possible
- Prefer early returns over nested conditionals

## Git
- Use conventional commit messages
- Never push to main directly

examples.title: Comprehensive personal preferences

code.content:

## Technical
- python3, not python
- Use gh CLI for GitHub operations
- Check for existing patterns before creating new abstractions

## Style
- Keep solutions simple, avoid over-engineering
- Use "humans" instead of "developers"

examples.explanation: Personal memory captures your unique working style across all projects.

tips: This file takes precedence over project CLAUDE.md for personal preferences

dual_wielder.longDescription: Having both a user-level (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md) and project-level (./CLAUDE.md) memory file gives you the best of both worlds. Your personal preferences apply everywhere while project-specific conventions override where needed. Claude merges both files, with project rules taking precedence when there's a conflict.
dual_wielder.whyItMatters: This separation of concerns keeps your global preferences from conflicting with team standards while still personalizing your experience.

howTo.summary: Create memory files at both the user level and project level.

steps.instruction: Create your global personal preferences file

code.content:
mkdir -p ~/.claude
echo '# My Preferences

- Be concise
- Use TypeScript' > ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md

steps.instruction: Create project-specific memory in your repo

code.content:
echo '# Project Config

- Use ESLint with Airbnb config
- Tests go in __tests__ folders' > ./CLAUDE.md

steps.instruction: Claude now automatically merges both when you work in this project

examples.title: Personal vs Project separation
examples.description: Keep personal style separate from team conventions

code.content:
# ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md (Personal)
- I prefer verbose variable names
- Always explain your reasoning

# ./CLAUDE.md (Project)
- Use company naming conventions
- Follow PR template requirements

examples.explanation: Claude applies both, with project taking precedence for conflicts.

tips: Use personal memory for how you like to work, project memory for team standards

well_organized.longDescription: Using markdown headers (##) to structure your CLAUDE.md transforms it from a flat list of notes into a navigable document. Well-organized memory helps Claude quickly find relevant information and understand the hierarchy of your instructions. Headers create semantic sections that Claude can reference contextually.
well_organized.whyItMatters: Structured content helps Claude parse and apply your instructions more accurately, especially as your memory file grows larger.

howTo.summary: Add level-2 (##) markdown headers to organize your CLAUDE.md into sections.

steps.instruction: Open your CLAUDE.md and add section headers

code.content:

- Use Playwright for E2E

deep_hierarchy.longDescription: Using nested headers (### or deeper) in your CLAUDE.md creates a detailed hierarchy that mirrors complex project structures. This is especially useful for large projects with multiple subsystems, where you need to organize related information at different levels of specificity.
deep_hierarchy.whyItMatters: Deep nesting lets you organize complex projects without overwhelming Claude with flat lists. It creates a logical tree structure.

howTo.summary: Add level-3 (###) or deeper headers to create subsections within your main sections.

steps.instruction: Add nested headers for detailed organization

code.content:

the_archivist.longDescription: Creating a CLAUDE.md with 5 or more distinct sections demonstrates comprehensive project documentation. This level of detail ensures Claude has thorough context about your codebase architecture, conventions, workflows, and any special considerations. A well-archived memory becomes an invaluable reference.
the_archivist.whyItMatters: Comprehensive documentation means fewer repeated explanations. Claude can answer questions and make decisions aligned with your established patterns.

howTo.summary: Expand your CLAUDE.md to include at least 5 major sections covering different aspects of your project.

steps.instruction: Create comprehensive sections covering all major aspects

code.content:

tips: Start with the sections you reference most often

code_keeper.longDescription: Including code blocks in your CLAUDE.md lets you embed actual examples, templates, or reference snippets that Claude can use as patterns. This is more powerful than describing code in prose because Claude can directly reference and replicate the exact syntax, formatting, and patterns you prefer.
code_keeper.whyItMatters: Code examples are unambiguous. Instead of describing your preferred patterns, you show them directly, ensuring Claude follows them exactly.

howTo.summary: Add fenced code blocks with language annotations to your CLAUDE.md.

steps.instruction: Add code examples using triple backticks with language identifiers

examples.title: Component template example
examples.explanation: Claude will follow this exact structure when creating components.

tips: Always specify the language after the opening backticks for syntax highlighting

list_builder.whyItMatters: Lists provide quick reference material. Claude can scan them efficiently when making decisions about naming, structure, or allowed patterns.

link_collector.whyItMatters: External references point Claude to authoritative documentation when you need to discuss specific APIs, libraries, or standards.

preference_keeper.longDescription: Documenting your personal coding preferences and style guide in CLAUDE.md ensures Claude writes code the way you like it. This includes naming conventions, formatting preferences, architectural patterns, and any other stylistic choices that make code feel like yours rather than generic AI-generated output.
preference_keeper.whyItMatters: Consistent style across your codebase reduces cognitive load and makes code reviews faster. Your preferences become Claude's defaults.

howTo.summary: Add a preferences or style section documenting how you like code written.

steps.instruction: Document your coding preferences clearly

code.content:
## My Code Style

### Naming
- Use camelCase for variables and functions
- Use PascalCase for classes and types
- Prefer descriptive names over abbreviations

### Formatting
- 2 spaces for indentation
- Always use semicolons
- Single quotes for strings

### Patterns
- Prefer early returns over nested conditions
- Use async/await instead of .then() chains
- Destructure objects in function parameters

examples.title: Comprehensive style guide

code.content:
## Code Preferences

### Always Use
- TypeScript strict mode
- Functional components in React
- Named exports over default exports
- Explicit return types on functions

### Never Use
- var (use const/let)
- Class components (use hooks)
- any type (be specific)
- Nested ternaries

### Prefer
- ?? over || for nullish coalescing
- optional chaining (?.) for deep access
- Array methods over for loops

examples.explanation: Clear preferences ensure code matches your style perfectly.

tips: Be specific - 'clean code' is vague, 'use early returns' is actionable

forbidden_patterns.longDescription: Documenting anti-patterns and things to avoid is just as important as documenting what to do. By explicitly telling Claude what NOT to do - patterns that caused bugs, deprecated approaches, or practices that don't fit your project - you prevent repeating past mistakes and maintain code quality.
forbidden_patterns.whyItMatters: Explicit prohibitions prevent Claude from suggesting solutions you've already rejected. This saves time and prevents technical debt.

howTo.summary: Add a section documenting patterns, practices, or approaches to avoid.

steps.instruction: Create a section listing forbidden patterns and why

code.content:
## Anti-patterns - DO NOT USE

### Code Patterns
- NEVER use `any` type in TypeScript
- AVOID nested callbacks - use async/await
- DON'T use mutable global state

### Architecture
- NEVER put business logic in React components
- DON'T create circular dependencies between modules
- AVOID God objects - split large classes

### Security
- NEVER log sensitive data (passwords, tokens)
- DON'T use string concatenation for SQL queries
- AVOID storing secrets in code or config files

examples.title: Project-specific prohibitions

code.content:
## Forbidden Patterns

### DO NOT:
- Use Redux (we migrated to Zustand)
- Import from @legacy/ packages (deprecated)
- Use moment.js (use date-fns instead)
- Add new dependencies without team approval
- Skip writing tests for bug fixes

### NEVER:
- Push directly to main branch
- Disable TypeScript strict mode
- Use console.log in production code

examples.explanation: Clear prohibitions prevent Claude from suggesting deprecated patterns.

tips: Explain why something is forbidden - it helps Claude understand the reasoning

environment_detector.longDescription: Including platform-specific instructions in your CLAUDE.md helps Claude adapt its suggestions to your operating system. This is crucial for shell commands, file paths, and tooling that differs between macOS, Linux, and Windows. Claude can then provide the right commands for your environment.
environment_detector.whyItMatters: Cross-platform differences cause subtle bugs. Environment awareness ensures Claude gives you commands and paths that actually work on your system.

howTo.summary: Add platform-specific notes or conditional instructions to your memory file.

steps.instruction: Document platform-specific commands and paths

code.content:
## Platform Notes

I'm on macOS (darwin).

### Shell Commands
- Use `open` not `xdg-open` for opening files
- Use `pbcopy`/`pbpaste` for clipboard
- Homebrew is at /opt/homebrew on Apple Silicon

### Paths
- Home directory: /Users/username
- Config: ~/Library/Application Support/

### Docker
- Docker Desktop on Mac uses VM
- Mount performance differs from Linux

examples.title: Comprehensive platform awareness

code.content:
## Environment

Platform: macOS Sonoma (darwin arm64)

### When running shell commands:
- Use `sed -i ''` not `sed -i` (BSD vs GNU)
- Use `brew install` for packages
- Python is `python3`, not `python`

### Docker notes:
- Containers run in Linux VM
- Use `host.docker.internal` for host access

### IDE: VS Code
- Settings sync enabled
- Use CMD not CTRL for shortcuts

examples.explanation: Platform details help Claude give you the right commands first time.

tips: Include architecture (arm64 vs x64) for more precise suggestions

conditional_memory.longDescription: Using conditional blocks in your CLAUDE.md lets you create context-aware instructions that apply only in specific situations. This advanced pattern enables sophisticated rules like 'when working on tests, use this style' or 'if creating a new component, follow this template' without cluttering your general instructions.
conditional_memory.whyItMatters: Conditional rules keep your memory file focused. Instead of listing every exception, you create smart rules that activate when relevant.

howTo.summary: Add conditional statements using When/If/Only when patterns in your CLAUDE.md.

steps.instruction: Create conditional rules that apply in specific contexts

code.content:
## Conditional Rules

When working on test files:
- Use describe/it blocks from Jest
- Mock external dependencies
- Aim for one assertion per test

When creating new React components:
- Start with the interface definition
- Export as named export
- Add JSDoc comment for props

If modifying database schemas:
- Always create a migration file
- Never modify existing migrations
- Update TypeScript types after migration

examples.title: Context-aware rules

code.content:
## Smart Rules

When fixing a bug:
- Write a failing test first
- Reference the issue number in commit
- Add to CHANGELOG.md

When refactoring:
- Ensure tests pass before and after
- Keep commits atomic
- Don't change behavior

Only when working in /packages/legacy/:
- Use CommonJS, not ESM
- Class components are acceptable
- Don't introduce new dependencies

examples.explanation: Conditional rules apply the right standards based on context.

tips: Keep conditions specific enough to be useful but not so specific they never match

importer.longDescription: The @import syntax in CLAUDE.md lets you include content from other files, keeping your main memory file clean while still having access to extensive documentation. This is powerful for including generated content, shared team rules, or detailed reference material without bloating your primary configuration.
importer.whyItMatters: Imports let you organize extensive documentation across multiple files while maintaining a clean, focused main CLAUDE.md.

howTo.summary: Use @import statements to include content from other markdown files.

steps.instruction: Create separate documentation files to import

code.content:
mkdir -p .claude/docs
echo '# API Reference\n\nEndpoint documentation...' > .claude/docs/api.md

steps.instruction: Add @import statements to your CLAUDE.md

code.content:
# Project Config

## Core Rules
- Use TypeScript
- Follow REST conventions

## Detailed Documentation
@import .claude/docs/api.md
@import .claude/docs/architecture.md

examples.title: Modular documentation setup
examples.explanation: Imports bring in detailed docs without cluttering the main file.

tips: Use relative paths from the CLAUDE.md file location

multi_import.longDescription: Using @import to include 3 or more external files demonstrates advanced memory organization. This pattern is essential for large projects where you want to maintain separate documentation for different subsystems, team guidelines, and reference material while still having it all accessible to Claude.
multi_import.whyItMatters: Multiple imports scale your documentation without sacrificing organization. Each concern lives in its own file.

howTo.summary: Add at least 3 @import statements to include different documentation files.

steps.instruction: Create multiple focused documentation files

code.content:
mkdir -p .claude/docs
echo '# Frontend Guide' > .claude/docs/frontend.md
echo '# Backend Guide' > .claude/docs/backend.md
echo '# DevOps Guide' > .claude/docs/devops.md

steps.instruction: Import all files from your CLAUDE.md

examples.title: Comprehensive import structure
examples.explanation: Six imports create a comprehensive knowledge base from focused files.

tips: Consider using a docs/ folder for generated or frequently updated content

rule_maker.longDescription: Creating a .claude/rules/*.md file establishes a modular rules system for your project. Unlike putting everything in CLAUDE.md, rule files let you organize guidelines by topic, making them easier to maintain and share. Each rule file focuses on a specific concern like security, testing, or code style.
rule_maker.whyItMatters: Modular rules are easier to maintain, review, and share with teammates. Each concern has its own focused file.

howTo.summary: Create a markdown file in the .claude/rules/ directory with focused guidelines.

steps.instruction: Create the rules directory structure

code.content: mkdir -p .claude/rules

steps.instruction: Create your first rule file

code.content:
# Code Style Rules

## Naming Conventions
- Components: PascalCase
- Files: kebab-case
- Variables: camelCase

## Formatting
- 2-space indentation
- 100 character line limit
- Trailing commas in multiline

examples.title: Security rules file

code.content:
# Security Rules

## Authentication
- All endpoints require authentication
- Use JWT tokens with 1-hour expiry
- Refresh tokens stored in httpOnly cookies

## Data Handling
- Never log PII or credentials
- Use parameterized queries for all database operations
- Validate all user input with Zod schemas

## Dependencies
- No packages with known vulnerabilities
- Review new dependencies before adding

examples.explanation: Focused rule files are easier to audit and update.

tips: Claude automatically reads all .md files in .claude/rules/

modular_mind.longDescription: Organizing your rules into multiple files (3+) in the .claude/rules/ directory demonstrates sophisticated memory management. This pattern separates concerns cleanly - security rules in one file, testing conventions in another, code style in a third. Claude automatically reads all rule files, combining them with your CLAUDE.md.
modular_mind.whyItMatters: Modular organization scales with your project. New team members can add rules for their area without touching other files.

howTo.summary: Create at least 3 separate rule files in .claude/rules/ directory.

steps.instruction: Create multiple focused rule files

code.content:
mkdir -p .claude/rules
echo '# Testing Rules' > .claude/rules/testing.md
echo '# Security Rules' > .claude/rules/security.md
echo '# API Design Rules' > .claude/rules/api.md

steps.instruction: Add content to each rule file

- Every bug fix needs a regression test
- Use factories for test data
- Mock external services in unit tests

examples.title: Complete rules directory

code.content:

# code-style.md
# database.md

# testing.md

examples.explanation: Five focused rule files provide comprehensive, organized guidance.

tips: Name files descriptively so their purpose is clear at a glance

rule_library.longDescription: Creating 5 or more rule files in your .claude/rules/ directory establishes a comprehensive rule library. This level of organization is ideal for large teams or complex projects where different aspects of the codebase have distinct guidelines. Your rule library becomes living documentation that actively guides development.
rule_library.whyItMatters: A comprehensive rule library captures institutional knowledge. It's onboarding material, code review guidance, and architectural documentation combined.

howTo.summary: Create at least 5 rule files covering different aspects of your project.

steps.instruction: Plan your rule categories

code.content:
# Create a comprehensive rules structure
mkdir -p .claude/rules
touch .claude/rules/{code-style,testing,security,api-design,database}.md

steps.instruction: Populate each file with domain-specific rules
steps.note: Each file should focus on one area with 5-15 specific rules

tips: Review and update rules quarterly to keep them relevant

template_master.longDescription: Using template variables like {{variable}} in your CLAUDE.md enables dynamic content that Claude can interpret contextually. While not interpolated automatically, these placeholders communicate structure and indicate where values should vary, making your templates more useful as patterns.
template_master.whyItMatters: Template variables make your examples more generic and reusable. They show Claude where to substitute context-specific values.

howTo.summary: Add template placeholders using {{variableName}} syntax in your examples.

steps.instruction: Add template variables to make patterns reusable

examples.title: API endpoint template
examples.explanation: Template variables show Claude where to customize when generating new code.

tips: Use consistent naming like {{ResourceName}} for classes and {{resourceName}} for files

memory_curator.longDescription: Being a Memory Curator means actively maintaining and updating your CLAUDE.md based on new learnings. When you discover something that should be remembered - a pattern that works well, a pitfall to avoid, or a new convention - you add it to your memory file, making Claude smarter for future sessions.
memory_curator.whyItMatters: Active curation means your Claude experience improves over time. Each learning becomes a permanent improvement.

howTo.summary: Ask Claude to update your CLAUDE.md when you discover something worth remembering.

steps.instruction: When you learn something useful, ask Claude to remember it

code.content:
User: That approach worked great! Add a note to CLAUDE.md 
that we should prefer Zod over Yup for validation.

steps.instruction: Claude updates your memory file accordingly

code.content:

### Validation
- Use Zod over Yup - better TypeScript inference

examples.title: Curating lessons learned

code.content:

with tree shaking. Add this to our forbidden patterns.

Claude: I'll add that to CLAUDE.md under anti-patterns:

- Avoid barrel exports (index.ts re-exports) - breaks tree shaking

examples.explanation: Each learning session improves Claude's future suggestions.

tips: Review and prune your memory periodically to keep it focused

memory_archaeologist.longDescription: A Memory Archaeologist documents learnings from past conversations in their CLAUDE.md. When you reference previous sessions - what worked, what failed, why you made certain decisions - you create institutional memory that benefits all future work, even when the original context is long forgotten.
memory_archaeologist.whyItMatters: Past context often explains present decisions. Documenting it preserves the 'why' behind your code and conventions.

howTo.summary: Document learnings and decisions from past Claude sessions in your CLAUDE.md.

steps.instruction: Add a section for historical learnings

code.content:
## Historical Decisions

### Why We Use X Instead of Y
(2024-03-15) We tried using Redux but found it too
verbose for our needs. Switched to Zustand which
reduced boilerplate by 60%.

### Database Choice
(2024-01) Selected PostgreSQL over MongoDB because
our data is highly relational and we need ACID
compliance for financial transactions.

## Decision History

Evaluated: JWT vs Sessions

tips: Date your entries so you know when decisions were made
